rationale: B wins because it turns the launch's two real weak spots — reliability and usage billing — into sharper reporter assignments. Its best line, "does a user pay for the attempts that fail?", is a real business-tech question; A's comparable pricing frame, "what do you charge for when the labor is metered compute rather than a logged-in human?", is smarter than average but drifts into conference-panel fog. B loses points for inventing "hobbyists," so this is not a clean win.
gaps_in_A: "the whole software industry is arguing about" is an unsupported trend claim. The update gives usage-based pricing, not evidence of a broad industry fight.
"When the software writes itself, you pay by the job" overstates the pricing fact. The update says usage-based on top of subscriptions; it does not say job-based billing.
"lands ahead of course planning for the coming academic year" is plausible timing, but it is not supplied. Fine as an inference if labeled; too neat as a hard peg.

The next step pushes `newsjack-detector` for a current signal even though the launch itself is the supplied news event. The first move should be proof: reliability, education availability, and named users.
gaps_in_B: "tens of millions of hobbyists" is invented. The update says tens of millions of users and positioning for non-engineers/vibe coders; it does not say those users are hobbyists.
"the same product will land in the accounts schools already use" assumes education-account availability. The set later asks whether it is enabled, so it knows this is unproven.
"repositioning from a place to learn coding into a place where non-engineers ship apps" overstates the company shift from one launch. Good instinct, sloppy proof posture.
Pricing and data angles both live off the same undisclosed reliability hole. They are different enough to keep, but the set should admit the overlap more aggressively.
